questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t\ge 0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{t/3}-1.$ At time $t=0$ the particle is located at the position $x=e+1.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=3?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=3$ is equal to its position at $t=0$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [0,3].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(3)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{3}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(3) & =(e+1)+{\int }_{0}^{3}({e}^{t/3}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =e+1+{[3{e}^{t/3}-t]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =e+1+([3{e}^{(3)/3}-(3)]-[3{e}^{(0)/3}-(0)]) \\  & =e+1+([3e-3]-[3]) \\  & =e+1+3e-6 \\  & =4e-5.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=3$ is $x=4e-5.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)={e}^{t-1}.$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=2.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=2?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=2$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,2].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(2)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{2}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =2+{\int }_{1}^{2}{e}^{t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{[{e}^{t-1}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2+({e}^{2-1}-{e}^{1-1}) \\  & =2+({e}^{1}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =2+e-1 \\  & =e+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=2$ is $x=e+1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Final Position of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis and its velocity at time $t>0$ is given by $v(t)=2t+{t}^{2}.$ At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=4.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=3?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=3$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,3].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(3)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{3}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Carrying out the computations, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(3) & =4+{\int }_{1}^{3}(2t+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =4+{[{t}^{2}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =4+([{3}^{2}+\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}]-[{1}^{2}+\frac{{1}^{3}}{3}]) \\  & =4+([9+9]-[1+\frac{1}{3}]) \\  & =4+(18-\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =4+\frac{50}{3} \\  & =\frac{62}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=3$ is $x=\frac{62}{3}.$

The graph above shows the velocity of an object moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis. At time $t=1$ the particle is located at the position $x=1.$ What is the position of the particle at time $t=6?$
questions.worked_solution:
The position of the particle at $t=6$ is equal to its position at $t=1$ plus the total displacement over $t\in [1,6].$ Therefore, we can calculate it as follows:

$$
x(6)=x(1)+{\int }_{1}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

We are told that $x(1)=1$, and we can compute the integral ${\int }_{1}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t$ by finding the signed area under the graph from $t=1$ to $t=6.$ Computing the signed area, we get

$$
{\int }_{1}^{6}v(t)\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(6)=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=6$ is $x=\frac{3}{2}.$

$$
x(5)=x(2)+{\int }_{2}^{5}v(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

We are told that $x(2)=-4.5$, and we can compute the integral ${\int }_{2}^{5}v(t)\,\text{d}t$ by finding the signed area under the graph from $t=2$ to $t=5.$ Computing the signed area, we get

$$
{\int }_{2}^{5}v(t)\,\text{d}t=3.5.
$$

Therefore,

$$
x(5)=-4.5+3.5=-1.
$$

So the position of the particle at $t=5$ is $x=-1.$
